A Letter Written in Your Cells: DNA, the Language of Life
Your eyes saw my body. In your book they were all written, the days that were ordained for me, when as yet there were none of them. (Psalm 139:16)
Introduction: You Are a Walking Book

Peace to you, brothers and sisters! To begin today, I want to ask you to do something very simple: look at your left hand, then look at your right hand. Good. Now I have an astonishing announcement: what you are holding right now is not just a pair of hands. It is a library.

Someone is thinking, “Pastor, I hardly ever read books. How did I become a library?” Hold on. Today we are walking into the first exhibit room of the Life Hall in “Creation Speaks,” and our topic is “DNA: The Language of Life.”

Inside almost every cell of your body is an instruction manual written in just four letters. The human genome has about 3 billion base pairs. What does that mean? If one book held three million letters, then printing your whole manual would fill about 1,000 books.

So when I say you are a walking library, I am not exaggerating in the least. Every morning you get up, brush your teeth, run for the bus and scroll your phone, and all the while you are carrying a thousand books around the city. The next time someone says you have “no depth,” you can answer with great confidence, “I carry a thousand books, a full set in every single cell.”

Even more amazing, if the DNA in a single cell were stretched out straight, it would be about 2 meters long, taller than most of us sitting here. Yet this two-meter thread is neatly packed into a nucleus far smaller than the tip of a pin.

When I put my earphone cord in my pocket for five minutes, it comes out tied in a hopeless knot. But the DNA in your body, two meters long, is stored in a space far smaller than a pinpoint, and when it is needed, the cell can still find exactly the passage it has to read. That is not a master of tidying. That is a miracle of tidying.

David, who wrote this psalm, did not know what DNA was, but moved by the Holy Spirit he wrote, “Your eyes saw my body. In your book they were all written, the days that were ordained for me, when as yet there were none of them.” Today we are going to start from this “book” and come to know the God who wrote it.
1. A Language Written in Four Letters
The meaning is in the arrangement

First, let’s look at what script this book is written in. Chinese has thousands of common characters, and English has twenty-six letters. So how many letters does DNA use? The answer is four. A, T, C and G, four bases. That is all.

You might think, “Only four letters? What could you possibly write with that?” But think about a computer. A computer uses only two symbols, 0 and 1, and with them it writes movies, music and every photo on your phone. The point is not how many letters there are, but how they are arranged. The meaning of DNA is hidden in the order of its letters.

DNA even has grammar. Every three bases form a “codon,” just as three letters can form a word. Four letters in groups of three give 64 combinations, which correspond to 20 amino acids plus “stop” signals.

Look, it even has punctuation! When the cell reads a “stop” codon, it is like reading a period, telling the cell, “This sentence is finished; this protein is done.” This is not a pile of gibberish. It is a language with letters, with vocabulary and with periods.
What a recipe book teaches us
The App has a great analogy: DNA is like a recipe book. The paper and ink are chemicals, but how to cook a dish is not found in the chemistry of the ink; it is found in the arrangement of the words.

My mother has a handwritten recipe book with her famous braised pork. If you took that page to a lab for analysis, all you would get is paper fiber and ink composition. You would never find the recipe for braised pork in the lab results. Where is the recipe? It is in the arrangement of the words, in the heart and intention of the one who wrote them.
Rearrange the same four letters, and you write an entirely different living thing. An apple tree, a puppy, you and I all use the same set of letters; the difference is in what is written.
Scripture: In the beginning was the Word
This brings to mind the opening line of the Gospel of John:
In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God. (John 1:1)
All things were made through him. Without him, nothing was made that has been made. (John 1:3)

The “Word” is God’s speech. From its very first page, the Bible tells us that God created the world by speaking. God said, “Let there be light,” and there was light. And today, when scientists open up the deepest layer of life and discover that inside it is a language, isn’t that astonishing?
People write to express what is on their hearts. When we discover that the foundation of life is a language, we cannot help asking: who wrote this text?
Two complementary strands, like a photo negative

Our second point is how this book gets copied. In 1953, Watson and Crick published their double-helix model of DNA in the journal Nature. Interestingly, at the end of the paper they added one understated sentence, saying in effect that this pairing immediately suggested a way the genetic material could be copied.

That sentence was understated, but it carried great weight. DNA is two chains wound around each other, and A always pairs with T, C always with G. What does that mean? It means each strand is the negative of the other.

Those of us who are a little older remember film negatives. With a negative, you can print an identical photograph. DNA works the same way: separate the two strands, and each one can rebuild its other half by the pairing rules. So when a cell divides, the manual can be copied accurately for the next generation.
Reading takes a whole translation team
But having a book is not enough; someone has to read it. To read DNA, the cell first transcribes the needed passage into RNA, and then ribosomes translate it, word by word, into protein.

It is like a large company whose confidential files at headquarters cannot be checked out, so a copy is made and handed to a translator at the factory, who uses it to make the product. And here is the amazing part: the entire reading and translation team is itself built from the instructions in DNA.

It is like a book that contains instructions for building a machine that reads that very book. The book needs the machine to read it, and the machine has to be built from the book. Brothers and sisters, a design like that makes you stop and marvel.

In 2022, an international team published the first complete, gap-free human genome sequence, from telomere to telomere. In other words, it took humanity nearly seventy years to read this book from cover to cover for the first time, without a single missing page.

Scientists have also found that they can encode books and images into synthetic DNA and then read them back out. That shows DNA is an extraordinarily dense medium for storing information. The most advanced storage technology humans can dream of wants to borrow the very system God placed in our cells long ago.

We also need to be honest: how much of the genome’s “non-coding” regions, the parts that do not directly make proteins, actually has a function is still being researched and debated. We do not need to exaggerate. Science still has plenty of homework to do, and that is part of what makes it so fascinating.

Back in Psalm 139, David says, “In your book they were all written, the days that were ordained for me, when as yet there were none of them.” David was writing about God knowing all the days of our lives; today we see that even our bodies have a book that has been written.
I will give thanks to you, for I am fearfully and wonderfully made. Your works are wonderful. My soul knows that very well. (Psalm 139:14)

In the past, when we read “fearfully and wonderfully made,” we may have thought only that the body is intricate. Reading it again today, are you a little more moved? We are made so wonderfully that even the tiniest cell contains an entire language.
Our third point asks a deeper question: where does such precise information come from?

In everyday life, every piece of coded information with a specific meaning, whether a letter, a piece of computer code or a recipe, comes from a mind. If you saw the words “I love you” spelled out in the sand on a beach, you would never say the waves happened to wash them up. You would ask, “Who wrote this?”

So it is reasonable for us to infer that the information in DNA points to an author with a mind. But let’s be clear: this is a philosophical inference, not a fact directly proven by experiment. Some scholars hold that information can arise gradually through natural processes. We respect different views, but we can also say with confidence that this inference is reasonable, and that it fits beautifully with what the Bible reveals.
You are not a pile of random letters

Brothers and sisters, this is not just an academic question. It shapes how you see yourself. If you were only a pile of randomly arranged letters, your existence would have no meaning, like a sheet of paper scattered by the wind.
But the Bible tells us that God created the world by speaking, and He also wrote an instruction manual into your cells. You are not a pile of random letters; you are a work written with care.

Some people feel like a failure, like they are unnecessary, like “I’m an essay that was written wrong.” But the One who wrote you saw you before you were formed. He does not write rough drafts to throw away; every piece He writes carries His intention.
The God who wrote your body has also written His purpose for your life

The even better news is that the One who wrote the manual for your body has also written His purpose for your life. He gave you not only DNA but also the Bible. He not only keeps you alive; He wants you to know what you are living for.

The Gospel of John says, “In the beginning was the Word,” and then later, “The Word became flesh.” The Word who wrote all things entered the very story He had written. That is Jesus Christ. The Author stepped into His own book to bring His lost readers home. That is the gospel.
In the 321 vision, one of the three foundations is “the Bible is my standard.” DNA is the manual for the body; the Bible is the manual for life.

Think about it: what would happen if a cell did not follow DNA’s instructions? Proteins would be made wrong, and the body would run into trouble. In the same way, if we do not live by the Bible, our lives will malfunction. Many people’s lives go wrong not because they don’t try hard enough, but because they are not following the manual. Only when we live by it does life work the way it should.
Change your mindset, change your life

The second application is “changing our mindset.” Today we learned a lot of information: 3 billion base pairs, 64 codons, the double helix. But if all of this stays at the level of “information,” at best it makes us a little more learned.

We need to move from “information” to “revelation,” letting the Holy Spirit light up what we learned today so it becomes knowledge of God. We move from a human perspective to God’s perspective: human eyes look at DNA and see chemistry; the eyes of faith see the wisdom of an Author.
Let Jesus receive all the glory
The third application is one of the core convictions of 321: let Jesus receive all the glory. My existence is His work, not my own achievement.

It is easy to treat our intelligence, health or looks as our own accomplishments. But of the thousand books you carry, you did not write a single word. When someone praises you, you can say in your heart, “Lord, this is Your work. The glory belongs to You.”

This week, please read a passage of Scripture each day, copy out one sentence as a “code” written into your life, and try to live it out that same day. Just as DNA is transcribed into RNA and then translated into protein, God’s word needs to be copied from the page into our hearts and then “translated” into our actions.

Brothers and sisters, please place your hand on your chest. Right now, tens of trillions of cells in your body are reading, transcribing and translating that manual, without stopping for a moment. You haven’t thought about them today, but they haven’t forgotten their work for a single second.

And the God who wrote this manual has not forgotten you for a single second either. Let us quietly reflect: The One who wrote the manual for my body has also written His purpose for my life. Am I willing to read the words He has written to me?

Lord, Creator of all things, You knew me before I was formed. Thank You for writing my life with wisdom. Please write Your word on the tablet of my heart too, so that I may live according to Your purpose. In Jesus’ name, Amen.

The Invisible City: Division of Labor and Cooperation in the Cell
Yahweh, how many are your works! In wisdom, you have made them all. The earth is full of your riches. (Psalm 104:24)
Introduction: A City You Carry with You Every Day

Peace to you, brothers and sisters and friends! If I asked you which is the busiest city you have ever visited, some of you would say Taipei, others Kuala Lumpur, Shanghai or Singapore. Those cities have subways, power plants, post offices, libraries and convenience stores that never close.
But today I want to tell you that the busiest, most finely tuned city is not on any map. It is in you. More precisely, it is in every single cell of your body.

A typical human cell is only a fraction of the width of a hair, completely invisible to the naked eye. But if we could shrink down and walk inside, we would find a city: walls and gates, a library, power plants, factories, a post office, roads and even recycling centers.

This city holds an enormous number of protein molecules, each doing its own job, working without pause. They take no vacations, never clock in and never complain about overtime. If you overslept this morning, they didn’t. If you are nodding off during this sermon, they certainly are not.

The writer of Psalm 104 saw the abundance of nature and could not help praising God: “Yahweh, how many are your works! In wisdom, you have made them all. The earth is full of your riches.” Today we want to say: not only is the earth full of God’s riches, but even a single invisible cell is full of God’s riches.
1. Division of Labor in the City: Every Department Has Its Place
Let’s tour this city stop by stop, like a group on a day trip.

Stop one: the walls and gates, which are the cell membrane. The membrane is a lipid bilayer only a few nanometers thick. It is unbelievably thin, yet remarkably wise. It is fitted with all kinds of channels and pumps that decide who may come in and who may go out. Like a conscientious security guard, it doesn’t block everything, and it doesn’t let everything through; it opens the gate selectively.

Stop two: the central library, which is the nucleus. This is where the DNA blueprints are kept. The library has one rule: the original blueprints never leave the building; only the page that is needed is copied into RNA and sent out. What a clever librarian. The precious original always stays in the library.

Stop three: the power plant, which is the mitochondrion. It converts the energy from the food we eat into ATP the cell can use. The bowl of beef noodles you had for lunch is right now being turned in your mitochondria into the energy you are using to listen to this sermon. So if someone dozes off in a minute, it may not be because the sermon is boring; the power plant is just busy processing lunch.
Factory, post office, roads and recycling center

Stop four: the factory and post office, which are the endoplasmic reticulum and the Golgi apparatus. They make and process proteins, then put an “address” label on them, package them and ship them out.

Stop five: the road system, which is the cytoskeleton. Its microtubules are like highways, and tiny porters called motor proteins walk along them carrying cargo. Picture it: highways running through your cells, with countless couriers hurrying along them. Isn’t that a lively scene?

The last stop: the recycling centers, which are the lysosomes and proteasomes. They break down damaged parts so the materials can be used again. It turns out the city God designed was recycling long before we were, and it is greener than we humans are.
Scripture: God arranged them as He desired

Brothers and sisters, have you noticed that no department in this city is unnecessary, and none can survive on its own? Without the library’s blueprints, the power plant wouldn’t know how to build itself; without the power plant’s energy, the library couldn’t operate.
But now God has set the members, each one of them, in the body, just as he desired. (1 Corinthians 12:18)
Every part has a place God has arranged. This is not only about cells; it is about each one of us.
2. The Miracle of the Postal Code: Crowded but Not Chaotic
How does a protein know where to go?
Our second point is a fascinating question: with so many proteins in the cell, how does each one know where to go to work?

The answer is that a newly made protein carries a short “signal sequence,” like a postal code, that determines where in the cell it will be delivered. This discovery won the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine in 1999.

It reminds me of sending greeting cards at New Year. If the address is wrong or the postal code is missing, the card may never arrive, or it may take a long detour to get there. But the proteins in a cell carry the correct address from birth and are delivered precisely to where they belong.

Cell biologists love to describe this city in numbers: the size, count and speed of its molecules. Those numbers show us one thing: the cell is extremely crowded, yet not at all chaotic. It is a highly ordered system.

It makes me think of a train station at rush hour. There are crowds of people, but if everyone knows which train to catch and which exit to take, the whole station is crowded but orderly. Let just one person stand still at the top of the escalator, though, and everything behind them jams up. The order in a cell is better than the best train station.
Still, we need to be honest: “the cell is like a city” is a helpful analogy, but the way cells organize themselves is not exactly the same as a human-built city.

The App puts it well: a cell is like a city not because it matches a city in every detail, but because both face the same challenges: supplies must come in, waste must go out, messages must be passed along, and every department must keep to its post and work with the others. We use analogies to help us understand, not to exaggerate.
Spiritual meaning: He is the God of details
So we see that God’s wisdom is displayed not only in the magnificent starry sky but also in the tiny places we cannot see. He is the God of great things and the God of details.

Sometimes we feel that God only handles the big things, like national affairs and world events, and that He probably has no time for my little worries. But brothers and sisters, God has arranged even the address of a single protein in your cells. How could He not care about the details of your life?
3. The Body of Christ: Each Part Doing Its Work, Helping One Another
The cell is a system, and so is the church

Our third point moves from the cell to the church. The cell’s departments depend on one another and work in coordination, displaying an overall order and purposefulness. That makes it reasonable for us to infer that there is a wise Designer behind it. This is a philosophical inference, but the direction it points is very clear.
Even more interesting, the Bible’s description of the body of Christ is also a picture of cooperation and shared work:

from whom all the body, being fitted and knit together through that which every joint supplies, according to the working in measure of each individual part, makes the body increase to the building up of itself in love. (Ephesians 4:16)

Look at this verse. It is almost a description of a cell. “Fitted and knit together” means the departments are connected to one another; “every joint supplies” means each organelle does its own job and contributes; “the working in measure of each individual part” means they provide for one another; and “makes the body increase” means the whole organism grows in health.
When the mitochondrion wants to be the nucleus

Let’s imagine a funny scene. One day the mitochondrion gets fed up and says, “Why do I have to generate power all day, working so hard, while the nucleus gets to sit in the library reading books? I want to be the nucleus too!”

So the power plant goes on strike, and the whole city loses power. Then the nucleus says, “I’m so important. Why should I live in the middle of the city and depend on others for my electricity?” So the library closes, and no blueprints go out. Before long, the whole city grinds to a halt.

Of course, real mitochondria don’t think like that. They quietly keep to the place God has given them. But what about us? Sometimes this very thing happens in the church: many people want to be up front, but few are willing to quietly set up chairs in the back; many envy other people’s gifts, but few treasure their own place.

Brothers and sisters, in God’s household, which department are you? Maybe you are a greeter, the “city gate” who is the first to welcome newcomers. Maybe you are on the care team, the one who quietly “recycles” other people’s broken hearts. Maybe you handle the sound, the cleaning or the meals, like the roads and post office in a cell. No one notices, but without you, the whole fellowship would jam up.
God has set the members in the body just as He desired. Your place is not an accident; it is God’s arrangement.
One purpose of the 321 vision is to “build God’s kingdom system.” The cell is a system, and so is the church. Only when each person finds their place can the whole be healthy.

A system is not held up by one superhero; it depends on every person doing their part and helping one another. The pastor is not the whole cell, and the members are not an audience. Everyone is an essential department in this system.
The second application is “humility overcomes pride.” The mitochondrion does not try to be the nucleus. Return to our proper place: let people be people, and let God be God.

Pride often starts with comparison: “Why them and not me?” Humility starts with gratitude: “Lord, thank You for giving me this place.” When we return to our proper place, we stop being busy comparing ourselves with others and focus on doing well what God has entrusted to us.
The third application is “people matter more than tasks.” The city runs for the sake of life, not for the sake of running. Ministry is also for people, not for the program itself.

It is easy in ministry to become someone who only sees tasks: whether the event succeeded, whether the report looks good. But every department of the cell ultimately exists to sustain life. All of our ministry also exists so that people may receive life.

This week, please find someone who serves quietly in your church or fellowship, thank them, and tell them, “Your place really matters.” Maybe it is the volunteer who opens the online meeting for everyone each week, or the sister who always prays for everyone right on time. A simple thank-you may be the most beautiful thing they hear all month.
Brothers and sisters, look at the palm of your hand. In every square centimeter of skin, thousands upon thousands of these cities are running, and today you have hardly given them a thought.
But God has been thinking about them all along, and He has been thinking about you all along. He has ordered even the smallest cell perfectly, and He can order your life too.
Let us quietly reflect: In God’s household, which “department” am I? Have I kept to the place God has given me?
God of wisdom, You have ordered even the smallest cell perfectly. Please order my life as well, so that in my family, my church and my workplace I do my part and help others. In Jesus’ name, Amen.

Who Generates the Power While You Sleep? Molecular Machines and the Lord Who Holds All Things Together
He is before all things, and in him all things are held together. (Colossians 1:17)
Introduction: A Factory Whose Lights Never Go Out

Peace to you, brothers and sisters! Let me start with a question: how many hours did you sleep last night? Some will say six, some eight, and someone will honestly admit, “I was binge-watching until two in the morning, so I only got four.”

Well, however long you slept, I want to tell you something: while you were sleeping, there was a factory in your body that did not rest at all. In this factory are countless tiny rotary motors, each only a few tens of nanometers across, and as they spin they produce the body’s energy currency, called ATP.

Even more astonishing, the ATP you make, use and recycle each day adds up to roughly your own body weight. If you weigh sixty kilograms, your body handles about sixty kilograms of ATP every day. And most of that ATP is spun out, one molecule at a time, by these little motors.
So the next time someone says, “I didn’t do anything today, and I’m so tired,” you can tell them, “Today your body spun out about your own weight in energy currency. Of course you’re tired!”

This is the third unit of the Life Hall, and our topic is “Molecular Machines.” We are going to see spinning motors and walking porters working day and night inside you. And we are going to see who is holding all of it together.
Colossians says, “He is before all things, and in him all things are held together.”
1. ATP Synthase: The Watermill in Your Cells
The first machine I want to introduce is called ATP synthase. The name sounds academic, but the way it works is actually a lot like something familiar.

Here is how it works: hydrogen ions flow through a channel in the membrane and turn a rotor; the rotating shaft changes the shape of the head; and the head joins ADP and phosphate together to make ATP. The whole process is like a hydroelectric generator.

The App uses a beautiful analogy: ATP synthase is like a watermill. The flowing water, the hydrogen ions, turns the waterwheel, the rotor; the wheel drives the millstone, the head; and the millstone grinds the grain into flour, the ATP.

Just how small is this mill? A million of them lined up in a row would stretch only about one centimeter. Take out a ruler and look at one centimeter: a million mills could fit along it. As children we read fairy tales about tiny elves with their own mills. It turns out they are real, and they are inside our bodies.
Seeing it spin with their own eyes
You might ask, “How can scientists know something so small is spinning? Are they just guessing?” No, they are not guessing.

In 1997, Japanese scientists came up with a clever method. They attached a fluorescent filament to the shaft of the F1 unit and then, under a microscope, watched it rotate with their own eyes! This confirmed the rotational catalysis mechanism proposed by Boyer, and Boyer received the Nobel Prize in Chemistry that same year.

I can imagine the atmosphere in the lab that day. A group of scientists crowded around the microscope, watching a tiny glowing filament begin to turn, and they must have shouted, “It really is spinning!” That is the beauty of science, and the beauty of creation.
These machines were not built and then left idle; they are running every second. While you sleep, they keep working. The Bible tells us who is holding all of this together:

His Son is the radiance of his glory, the very image of his substance, and upholding all things by the word of his power, when he had by himself made purification for our sins, sat down on the right hand of the Majesty on high. (Hebrews 1:3)

Notice the word “upholding.” It is ongoing. He did not make everything and then walk away; He keeps holding it up. Every heartbeat, every breath, every molecule of ATP is evidence of His faithfulness.
2. Kinesin: The Porter Who Walks with a Load on Its Back

The second machine is my favorite. It is called kinesin. It has two “feet” and walks step by step along the microtubules in the cell. Each step is about 8 nanometers, and each step uses one ATP, as it carries cargo throughout the cell.

Whenever I think of kinesin, I picture a tiny courier with a package bigger than itself on its back, walking along a thin track: left foot, right foot, left foot, right foot, faithfully marching on. It never says, “I’m too tired today; I’ll deliver the package tomorrow.” It just keeps walking, one step at a time.

This is not imagination either. Using a technique called “optical tweezers,” scientists tracked a single kinesin molecule and saw its “footsteps” as it moved forward. What Svoboda and colleagues observed were steps of about 8 nanometers.

Brothers and sisters, think about it: how precise an instrument did humans have to invent just to see the footsteps of one molecule? And that molecule has not stopped walking for a single day from the moment you were born until now.
Spiritual meaning: not walking for itself
The cargo kinesin carries is not for itself; it is delivered wherever the cell needs it. It spends its own energy so that the whole cell can live.
This reminds me of a spiritual principle: true life is not lived for oneself. Molecular machines do not turn for themselves but for the whole body. Paul says:
it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me. (Galatians 2:20)
This does not mean we lose ourselves. It means we find our true purpose: to live for Christ and for His body.
3. The Flagellar Motor: A Nano-Engine That Can Shift Gears
A motor on a bacterium’s tail

The third machine is the bacterial flagellar motor. At the base of an E. coli bacterium’s tail is a rotary motor about 45 nanometers across, built from about 20 kinds of parts. It can spin hundreds of times per second, and it can even change direction, turning forward or in reverse.

When we drive, we shift gears and back up; this bacterium’s motor can too. And building and operating the flagellum requires about 40 gene products, assembled in a precise order. It is like assembling a car: you don’t just toss the parts together and shake them; you install them one by one, in order.

At this point we need to be honest about a disputed question. A scholar named Behe argues that the flagellum is “irreducibly complex,” meaning it cannot work if any single part is missing. But other scholars, such as Pallen and Matzke, argue that the flagellum’s parts are related to other systems and may have developed gradually.

Brothers and sisters, the scientific community is still discussing this question. Our attitude is: unity on the core, generosity on the periphery. We don’t need to stake our faith on the outcome of any one scientific debate.

However the flagellum came to be, these molecular machines have engineering features such as motors, shafts and tracks, and they strongly display the appearance of design. That makes it reasonable to infer that there is a Designer behind them. This is a philosophical inference; we say so clearly, and we believe it with confidence.
In Colossians, Paul writes a magnificent passage:

For by him all things were created in the heavens and on the earth, things visible and things invisible, whether thrones or dominions or principalities or powers. All things have been created through him and for him. (Colossians 1:16)

“Things visible and things invisible.” Paul had no microscope, yet he knew that even the world we cannot see was created through Christ and for Him. Today, through science, we have seen these invisible, wonderful machines, and they bear out exactly what this verse says.
Let Jesus reign, instead of straining on our own
One of the two core convictions of 321 is “let Jesus reign.” All things hold together in Him, so my life should be under His rule too, not propped up by my own straining.

Many of us live exhausted, because deep down we think, “If I don’t hold it together, this family will fall apart; if I don’t hold it together, this job will be ruined.” But brothers and sisters, you can’t make even one motor in your own body turn. Do you really think you are the one holding your life together?
In fact, the Lord has been holding you up all along. When you admit that, you do not become weak; you are finally able to put down a burden you were never able to carry in the first place.
The second application is to give thanks in everything, giving the glory to the Lord who holds me up at every moment. Most of grace is unseen.

We often give thanks for visible blessings, like a raise, healing from an illness or a child getting into a good school. But have you ever thanked God for today’s ATP? For your heartbeat, your breathing and every porter quietly working in your body? The unseen graces far outnumber the ones we can see.
The third application is “selflessness.” Molecular machines do not turn for themselves but for the whole body. It is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me.

A selfless person is like a kinesin molecule, carrying what others need, walking step by step, seeking not their own glory but only the health of the body. People like that are the most beautiful blessing in a church.

This week, each night before bed, write down three graces that are “unseen but always at work,” and thank God for them. It might be your breathing, your family’s safety, or a friend who has been praying for you all along. After a week, you will find your list of thanks is much longer than you imagined.
Brothers and sisters, please take a deep breath. The oxygen you just breathed in is keeping countless rotary motors turning.
Breathe once more. That breath is not something you made; it is something the Lord upholds.
Let us quietly reflect: Do I often think that I am the one holding my life together?

Lord Jesus, all things hold together in You, and so do I. Thank You for holding me up every moment. Teach me to lay down the burdens I try to carry on my own and to trust in Your faithfulness. In Jesus’ name, Amen.

Origami in the Potter’s Hands: Protein Folding and the Shaping of a Life
But now, Yahweh, you are our Father. We are the clay and you our potter. We all are the work of your hand. (Isaiah 64:8)
Introduction: How Does a Thread Become a Paper Crane?

Peace to you, brothers and sisters! I wonder how many of you folded paper cranes as children. I did. I spent half an hour on one, and when I showed my mom what came out, she said, “What a cute chicken.”
Origami looks simple, but it is actually hard. To get it right, every crease has to be in the right place; get one fold wrong, and everything after it goes crooked.

Today I want to tell you that every second, countless acts of “origami” are going on inside your body, and almost every one of them is folded quickly and precisely. That is the theme of the fourth unit of the Life Hall: protein folding.

We learned earlier that the cell follows the instructions in DNA, linking amino acids together one by one into a long chain. But a straight chain can do nothing. It has to fold into a specific three-dimensional shape before it can become an enzyme, an antibody or a part of a muscle.

Even more amazing, many small proteins fold from a tangled thread into the right shape in less than a second, like an origami artist completing a paper crane in an instant. I spent half an hour and made a chicken; a protein takes less than a second and makes a crane. The gap is enormous.
Our key verse today is Isaiah 64:8: “But now, Yahweh, you are our Father. We are the clay and you our potter. We all are the work of your hand.”
1. Sequence Determines Shape, Shape Determines Function
The folding pattern is already written on the strip
Our first point: what determines the shape a protein finally folds into? The answer: the order of its 20 kinds of amino acids.

A scientist named Anfinsen performed a classic experiment. He unfolded a protein called ribonuclease so that it lost its shape, and found that it could refold on its own into its original shape. That showed one thing: the information for the shape is written in the amino acid sequence. For this he received the 1972 Nobel Prize in Chemistry.

The App has a helpful analogy: protein folding is like a strip of paper with the folding instructions already written on it. The creases are hidden in the sequence, and when you let go, it takes shape according to the pattern.

It is like buying a pop-up card with the fold lines already pressed in. When you open it, it snaps up on its own into a three-dimensional castle. The paper isn’t intelligent; the card’s designer pressed the fold lines into exactly the right places ahead of time.
Why does shape matter so much? Because shape determines function. On the surface of an enzyme is a pocket that fits exactly the molecule it acts on, like a key in a lock.

Have you ever stood at a door with a big ring of keys, trying them one by one, and only the eighth one worked? A key that is even slightly off won’t do. Proteins are the same: if the shape is even slightly off, the protein may lose its function completely.

So when proteins misfold, there are consequences. Misfolded or clumped proteins are linked to many diseases, including Alzheimer’s disease. This reminds us that the right shape is bound up with the health of life.
Scripture: You formed my inmost being
For you formed my inmost being. You knit me together in my mother’s womb. (Psalm 139:13)

While you were still in your mother’s womb, one precise act of origami after another had already begun in your body. Every enzyme and every antibody folded into the shape it should have. That is not our achievement; it is God’s covering care.
2. A Problem Longer Than the Universe, Solved by the Cell in a Second

Our second point is a problem that has given scientists headaches. A scientist named Levinthal pointed out that a protein chain has an astronomical number of possible shapes. If it had to try every possible shape one by one, it would take longer than the age of the universe.

It is like forgetting the combination to your suitcase lock and having to try every number from the beginning. If the lock had endless digits, you could keep trying until the end of the world and never open it.
Yet proteins fold in less than a second. So Levinthal concluded that folding must follow pathways; it cannot be random trial and error.

Scientists now have theories such as the “energy funnel” to explain this. You can picture water flowing down from the top of a funnel and naturally gathering at the lowest point. But the details are still being researched. We say honestly: science already knows a great deal, but it has not figured everything out.
Even artificial intelligence has to give it everything

The next part of the story is even more interesting. In 2020, AlphaFold, developed by the company DeepMind, reached near-experimental accuracy in the international protein structure prediction assessment. It was a major breakthrough.

Then in 2024, half of the Nobel Prize in Chemistry went to Hassabis and Jumper for their contributions to protein structure prediction, and the other half went to Baker for using computers to design new proteins.

Brothers and sisters, think about this: humans need cutting-edge artificial intelligence and massive computing power to predict how a protein will fold, yet the cells in your body accomplish it every second. That makes it reasonable for us to infer that such precision points to a wise Creator. Of course, this is a philosophical inference, not an experimental conclusion, but it is very persuasive.

I often think that scientists win Nobel Prizes because they have read and understood a little of the folding patterns God wrote long ago. If being able to read them deserves the applause of the whole world, how much praise does the One who wrote them deserve?
Spiritual meaning: the Potter knows how to fold
A protein has to fold into the right shape before it can do its work. Our lives are the same: we need to be shaped by God’s hands to become vessels fit for use.

We often think we get to decide the shape of our own lives. But just as a protein chain that folds any which way ends up with no function, when we fold our lives however we please, we often end up with a pile of problems. The One who truly knows what shape we should take is the Potter who made us.
3. Molecular Chaperones: God Uses the People Around Us to Help Us Take Shape
A little room for folding safely

Our third point is the part that moves me most. Scientists have found that some proteins cannot fold properly on their own; they need “chaperone” proteins beside them. These molecular chaperones keep proteins from misfolding or sticking to other proteins. Some chaperones are even like a little room where a protein can fold safely.
The App puts it warmly: molecular chaperones are like a patient teacher standing by to lend a hand so it does not fold crooked.

It reminds me of learning to ride a bicycle, with my dad running behind holding the bike. He didn’t ride it for me; he just steadied me when I was about to fall. Then one day I looked back and realized Dad had let go long ago, and I was already riding on my own.
God often walks with us through people
Molecular chaperones remind us that God often uses the people around us to walk with us as we are being formed.

On your journey of faith, have there been people like that? Maybe the small group leader who led you through Bible study, or the sister who prayed with you when you were at a low point, or the brother who spoke a hard truth when you were about to “fold crooked.” They are the “molecular chaperones” God placed beside you.
Scripture: the Potter who never gives up halfway
And God Himself is the Potter who never gives up halfway:
being confident of this very thing, that he who began a good work in you will complete it until the day of Jesus Christ. (Philippians 1:6)

Sometimes the process of being shaped is very uncomfortable. Pressure, waiting and brokenness can feel like being folded hard. But brothers and sisters, being folded does not mean being thrown away; being folded is exactly how we are shaped. The Potter’s hands may press firmly, but they are hands full of love. He who began a good work will complete it.
Life first, then relationships, then ministry

In the 321 vision there is a very important order: life first, then relationships, then ministry. A protein functions only after it has folded. When our lives are shaped first, our service bears fruit.

Many people, as soon as they come to faith, rush into all kinds of ministry. That zeal is precious. But if a life has not yet been shaped, it is like a protein chain that hasn’t finished folding: forcing it into use not only accomplishes nothing but may even cause problems. Let God shape your life first, and the fruit of your service will follow naturally.

The second application is 235 spiritual companions, walking closely with a few others in discipleship. Like a molecular chaperone, walk alongside a brother or sister and lend a hand while they are being shaped.

We don’t need to be anyone’s potter; that is God’s work. But we can be someone’s molecular chaperone, staying close beside them, steadying them when they are about to fold crooked, and praying for them.
Humility: let God be the Potter
The third application is humility. Let God be the Potter and me the clay, returning to our proper place as creatures.

The greatest wisdom of clay is not to argue with the potter. When we insist on keeping our own shape, we are saying, “I know better than You what I should look like.” Humility means putting ourselves in His hands and trusting that His hands are better than our ideas.

This week, please find a spiritual companion, share with each other one way “God is shaping me right now,” and pray for each other. It doesn’t have to be anything big. It might be pressure at work, or a relationship that requires waiting. Say it out loud, pray for each other, and you will become each other’s molecular chaperones.
Brothers and sisters, think back to a recent time when you felt “folded”: perhaps pressure, waiting or brokenness. It may be exactly how God is shaping you.

Every second, the proteins in your body are yielding to the folding pattern written in their sequence, taking on a shape that is beautiful and useful. Today, are you willing to yield to the Potter’s hands as well?
Let us quietly reflect: Am I willing to let God fold me into His pattern, or do I insist on keeping my own shape?

Father God, my Potter, I am the clay and You are the Potter. Shape me according to Your good pleasure, and send spiritual companions to walk with me as I am formed, so that I may become a vessel fit for the Master’s use. In Jesus’ name, Amen.

2. On your journey of faith, who has been a “molecular chaperone” for you? How did they steady you when you were about to fold crooked?
3. What experience of “being folded” are you going through right now? How are you willing to place it in the Potter’s hands?
The Chicken or the Egg? Where Did Life Come From?
For with you is the spring of life. In your light we will see light. (Psalm 36:9)
Introduction: A Question That Stumps Everyone
Peace to you, brothers and sisters! Today I want to begin with a question we have all argued about since childhood: which came first, the chicken or the egg?

I remember that in elementary school, our class split into two camps over this question. We argued through recess, and when class started we kept passing notes to continue the fight. Finally the teacher walked in and said, “Stop arguing. The teacher came first, so all of you sit down.”

Today we are going to talk about science’s version of the chicken-and-egg question, and it goes much deeper than that elementary-school debate. This is the fifth unit of the Life Hall: Where did life come from?

In the earlier units, we saw that DNA stores information and proteins do the work. But here is the problem: making proteins requires instructions from DNA, and reading DNA requires proteins. So how did the very first cell come about?
That is the chicken-and-egg puzzle of life. To this day, scientists are still working hard on it, and there is no agreed answer.
This is one of science’s deepest mysteries, and one of faith’s most fundamental questions. Psalm 36:9 says, “For with you is the spring of life. In your light we will see light.”
Today, let’s humbly look together at how scientists are exploring this question, and let’s also come to know with confidence the true source of life.
1. Lightning in a Flask: How Scientists Have Explored
Our first point looks at what scientists have tried. In 1953, a scientist named Miller carried out a famous experiment that later became known as the “Miller–Urey experiment.”

He placed water, methane, ammonia and hydrogen in a flask and then passed electric sparks through it to simulate lightning. The result? He obtained several amino acids. This experiment opened the era of experimental research into the origin of life.

Picture the scene: a flask crackling with flashes of electricity inside, like a miniature thunderstorm. After a while, scientists found that some of the raw materials that make up proteins had appeared. At the time it caused a real sensation.
A rediscovery half a century later

The story doesn’t end there. In 2008, scientists reanalyzed samples Miller had saved all those years before and identified 22 amino acids in one of his setups. Miller’s instruments back then could not see that clearly; only new technology decades later let those old samples tell us more.
I find this story charming, as if the scientists were opening a time capsule. It also shows that scientific research is carried forward from one generation to the next.
But things are not that simple. Many earth scientists think the early atmosphere may not have been as rich in reducing gases as Miller assumed. If that is so, it affects what the experiment means.

The App has a great analogy: going from amino acids to a cell is like going from a pile of bricks to a city with electricity, internet, libraries and factories. Getting the bricks is an important step, but the city is still a very long way off.

Friends, if you saw a pile of bricks at a construction site, would you say, “Wonderful, a city with a subway, hospitals and the internet will appear here any minute”? Bricks matter, but getting from bricks to a city takes far more than bricks.
2. The RNA World: A Key with Two Uses
Our second point looks at an important current line of research called the “RNA world hypothesis.”
Remember the chicken-and-egg puzzle? DNA stores information, proteins do the work, and each needs the other. So scientists wondered: is there a molecule that could play both roles at once?

They found that RNA seems to fit. RNA can both store information and catalyze reactions like an enzyme. So perhaps the earliest life used RNA, one molecule doing two jobs. It is like one person being both the chef and the recipe, so there is no need to argue about whether the chef or the recipe came first.
In 1986, Gilbert coined the term “RNA world.” Later scientists discovered that the catalytic core of the ribosome is RNA, which lent support to the idea.
But the origin-of-life chemist Orgel also acknowledged frankly that synthesizing RNA under non-living conditions, and getting it to copy itself, still faces many unsolved difficulties.

So the RNA world hypothesis is an important current line of research, but many chemical problems remain unsolved. Brothers and sisters, I really appreciate this kind of candor from scientists. Good scientists say, “This is what we know, and this is what we don’t know yet.”
The most honest answer for now
So what is the most accurate description of where science stands on how life emerged from non-living chemicals? Simply this: still under study, with no agreed explanation.
This is not Christians being contrary for the sake of it; it is the scientific community’s own honest assessment. Research continues, and there is no settled conclusion.
Our third point looks at the different views people hold on this question. The App summarizes three.

The first is chemical evolution research. Many scientists believe life emerged gradually under early-earth conditions through a series of chemical steps. They keep experimenting, hoping to fill in the gaps one step at a time.

The second is intelligent design. Some scholars argue that the coded information and precise systems life requires are best explained as coming from a designer with a mind. This is an inference at the boundary of philosophy and science.

The third is creation and secondary causes. Some Christian scholars hold that even if natural steps are discovered in the future, they would be processes God established and sustains. Whatever the means, God is the source of life.
Unity on the core, generosity on the periphery
Brothers and sisters, when we face these different views, our attitude is: unity on the core, generosity on the periphery.

What is the core? God is the source of life. What is the periphery? The means God used and the process involved. On peripheral questions, Christians who love the Lord may see things differently. We can respect one another; we don’t need to condemn one another.

Life requires information, machines and precise integration, and the best explanation for these appearing together is a life-giving Creator. That is our reasonable inference, a philosophical inference; scholars who see it differently look to future scientific explanations. We can hold our convictions gently and firmly while respecting other people’s search.

In fact, science and the Bible are answering questions on two different levels here. Science is still searching for the steps of “how” life began; the Bible tells us “from whom” life comes. These are questions on different levels, and they need not be enemies.

It is like asking, “How was this cake baked?” The answer is flour, eggs and oven temperature. But if you ask, “Who made this cake?” the answer is, “Mom made it for my birthday.” Both answers are true, but only the second lets you feel the love.
When Paul preached to the intellectuals of Athens, he said:

The God who made the world and all things in it, he, being Lord of heaven and earth, doesn’t dwell in temples made with hands. He isn’t served by men’s hands, as though he needed anything, seeing he himself gives to all life and breath and all things. (Acts 17:24–25)
Life is not something we earn; it is something we receive. You did not apply to be born, and you did not pay for the right to breathe. Life, breath and all things are given freely by God to everyone.
Deeper still, Jesus gives us not only physical life but eternal life:
In him was life, and the life was the light of men. (John 1:4)
Facing unsolved mysteries, we can humbly say, “We don’t know yet.” But about the source of life, we can say with confidence, “It is with You.”
The first application is “humility overcomes pride.” Admitting “we don’t know yet” is honesty in science and humility in faith. Let God be God.

Some Christians are afraid to say “I don’t know,” as if saying it means losing. It doesn’t. Admitting our limits is exactly how we leave the infinite to God. Proud people need to have an answer for everything; humble people know who the answer is.
The second application is “people matter more than tasks.” When you discuss this with friends who see things differently, respecting them matters more than winning the debate.

We might win a debate and lose a friend. That is not victory; that is defeat. The gospel does not spread by who shouts loudest, but by love and sincerity. Listen first, then share, and let the other person feel that you truly care about them, not that you only want to prove them wrong.
From the temporary to the eternal
The third application is “changing from the temporary to the eternal.” Physical life is limited, but the life Jesus gives lasts forever.

Scientists study the beginning of life; what Jesus gives us is life that never ends. Today’s question is not only “Where did life come from?” but also “Where is my life going?” And the answer is the same: it is with Him.

This week, please ask a friend, “Where do you think life came from?” Listen first, then gently share why you believe life is a gift from God. You don’t need to be a science expert; you just need to be a sincere friend.
Brothers and sisters, be still for a moment and notice your breathing and your heartbeat. This life is a gift you have been given.
Scientists may need many more years to answer how life began. But today you can already answer a more important question: Who gave me this life? And how will I respond to the Lord who gives life?
Let us quietly reflect: Do I treat my life as my own property, or as a gift received from God?
Source of life, my life, my breath and all things are given by You. Let me not merely have physical life, but live the abundant life in Jesus. In Jesus’ name, Amen.
1. Miller’s experiment produced amino acids, but there is still a long way to go “from bricks to a city.” How does this analogy help you understand where origin-of-life research stands today?

2. Of the three views, chemical evolution research, intelligent design, and creation and secondary causes, which one do you find easiest to accept? Under the principle of “unity on the core, generosity on the periphery,” how can we get along with brothers and sisters who see it differently?
3. If a friend asked you, “Where did life come from?” how would you listen first and then gently share? Try practicing with each other once in your group.
Finding Home Without a Map: Butterflies, Migratory Birds and the God Who Guides
In all your ways acknowledge him, and he will make your paths straight. (Proverbs 3:6)
Introduction: A Pastor Who Gets Lost

Peace to you, brothers and sisters! Let me confess something first: I get lost very easily. Even with GPS, I still take the wrong exit. The GPS says, “In three hundred meters, turn right,” and I often turn right at two hundred meters, and then the GPS keeps gently saying, “Recalculating route.”
My wife says the sentence I hear most often in my life is “Recalculating route.”

But today I want to introduce a few “navigation masters.” They have no phones, no maps and no one to teach them, yet they fly across mountains and oceans to find a distant home. This is the sixth unit of the Life Hall: Wondrous Navigation.

Every autumn, monarch butterflies from eastern North America fly up to several thousand kilometers to spend the winter in the fir forests of the mountains of central Mexico. Remarkably, the generation that makes the journey has never been there, and their grandparents never came back to show them the way.

Imagine going abroad for the first time with no map, no guide, and no one ever telling you where your destination is, yet flying all the way to a particular mountain forest in another country and landing right on target. I have to make three phone calls just to find a friend’s house!

There is also a bird called the bar-tailed godwit. It takes off from Alaska and, without eating, drinking, stopping or resting, flies straight across the Pacific all the way to New Zealand. Tracked flights have exceeded 11,000 kilometers. When we take a long-haul flight, we get airline meals, movies and a chance to sleep; the godwit just keeps flapping its own wings the whole way.
Our key verse today is Proverbs 3:6: “In all your ways acknowledge him, and he will make your paths straight.”
1. The Monarch Butterfly: A Sun Compass with a Built-In Clock
Our first point is the secret of the monarch butterfly. How does it find its way?

Research has found that monarchs orient by the sun. But here is the problem: the sun’s position keeps changing through the day. In the morning it is in the east, at noon overhead, and in the evening in the west. If a butterfly looked only at the sun, it would fly in different directions in the morning and the afternoon.

So the monarch also needs a clock to correct for the sun’s changing position. And where is that clock? In its antennae! Merlin and colleagues found that the monarch’s biological clock is located in its antennae.

Even more interesting, when researchers disrupted the biological clocks in a monarch’s antennae, the butterflies flew in the wrong direction. Those two slender antennae turn out to be not just cute decorations but precision navigation instruments.
A backup compass for cloudy days

What about cloudy days when the sun can’t be seen? Experiments show monarchs can also sense the inclination of Earth’s magnetic field as an aid. This magnetic compass is an important helper when the sun cannot be seen, such as on cloudy days.

Look how thoughtful God’s design is: there is not only a main system but also a backup system. It is like when your phone battery dies: if you still have a paper map in your pocket, you feel a lot more at ease.
Scripture: the stork knows its seasons
The prophet Jeremiah made a striking lament:
Yes, the stork in the sky knows her appointed times. The turtledove, the swallow, and the crane observe the time of their coming; but my people don’t know Yahweh’s law. (Jeremiah 8:7)

Birds know when to fly and where to go, yet God’s people often lose their way. Jeremiah’s lament is not a rebuke of the birds but a call for people to return. Birds follow the instincts God placed in them and find their way home, but people often resist the call God has placed in our hearts.
2. Migratory Birds and Salmon: Seeing the Magnetic Field, Smelling Home

Our second point looks at migratory birds and salmon. Experiments in 1972 confirmed that European robins can sense Earth’s magnetic field to orient themselves. In other words, there is an invisible compass inside a bird’s body.

So how do they “see” the magnetic field? This is a hot research topic. One leading hypothesis is that a protein in the bird’s eye called cryptochrome, when struck by light, produces something called a “radical pair,” which is very sensitive to the direction of the magnetic field.

A 2021 study showed that cryptochrome 4 from a migratory bird is magnetically sensitive. But the full mechanism has yet to be confirmed. So we need to say honestly: that migratory birds can orient using Earth’s magnetic field is certain; exactly how they sense it is still under study.

Now consider the salmon. Salmon live at sea for several years and then return to the very river where they were born. As they get close, they recognize their home water by smell; out at sea, they may “remember” their birthplace by Earth’s magnetic field.

I love this picture. It is like someone who has worked far from home for many years, returning to the lane where they grew up, catching the smell of familiar home cooking, and knowing, “I’m home.” Salmon recognize home with their noses.
As for how salmon use the magnetic field at sea to remember their birthplace, that is also still under study. Scientists keep working on it, and we keep marveling.

The App has a vivid analogy: these animals are like travelers carrying a built-in navigation system. The sun is the compass, a clock corrects the heading, the magnetic field is the backup compass, and smell is the house number for the last mile. No one teaches them, yet it is passed down accurately from generation to generation.

These precise navigation abilities, passed across generations without being learned, make it reasonable for us to infer that there is a Creator who gave His creatures wisdom. This is a philosophical inference, but it is a beautiful one.
Scripture: Is it by your wisdom?
In the book of Job, God asks Job a question:
Is it by your wisdom that the hawk soars, and stretches her wings toward the south? (Job 39:26)
The question is humorous and profound at the same time. It is as if God were saying, “Job, did you teach those birds to fly south?” Of course not. God placed that wisdom inside them.
What we need is not a better map
Our third point turns from the birds to ourselves. God not only gave animals a compass; He also promises to guide us Himself:
I will instruct you and teach you in the way which you shall go. I will counsel you with my eye on you. (Psalm 32:8)
Notice the words “with my eye on you.” God does not hand you a map and tell you to find your own way; He keeps His eye on you the whole way, ready to remind you and counsel you.
That is better than any navigation system. Your phone’s GPS can only say “Recalculating route,” but God says, “My child, I am here. I will lead you.”
Trust with all your heart, not in your own understanding
Proverbs gives us a very clear principle:
Trust in Yahweh with all your heart, and don’t lean on your own understanding. In all your ways acknowledge him, and he will make your paths straight. (Proverbs 3:5–6)

The monarch butterfly does not rely on its own cleverness to find the way; it relies on the compass God placed in it. Our biggest problem is often that we trust our own cleverness too much. We think we see clearly, and we end up going the long way around.
Knowing only which way to fly next

There is one more thing that moves me. That small butterfly takes off in the autumn wind toward a faraway place it has never seen. It does not know the whole route; it only knows which way to fly for the next stretch.

Many times we are the same. We want God to tell us His five-year or ten-year plan for our lives all at once, but God often lets us see only the next step. That is not because God is stingy, but because He wants us to trust Him one step at a time. The monarch doesn’t need to see Mexico; it only needs to fly in the right direction. We don’t need to see everything; we only need to follow the Lord who sees everything.
The Holy Spirit is my guide

One of the three foundations of 321 is “the Holy Spirit is my guide.” The monarch relies on its built-in compass; the Christian relies on the leading of the Holy Spirit. Pray and seek Him first in everything.

Very often we make a decision first and pray afterward; sometimes we only think to pray after it is done and something has gone wrong. Letting the Holy Spirit guide us means putting prayer first: ask God first, then take off.
Lead with a Spirit-led heart, not a self-reliant head

The second application: lead with a Spirit-led heart, not a self-reliant head. This does not mean we stop thinking; it means we do not lean on our own understanding but trust in Yahweh with all our heart.

Our minds are a good gift from God, but they are not our master. Just as the clock in the monarch’s antennae corrects its heading by the sun, we need the Holy Spirit to correct our thinking, changing from a human perspective to God’s perspective.
Faithfulness: guidance from generation to generation
The third application is faithfulness. God passes navigation down to His creatures generation after generation, and He leads His people generation after generation.

The generation of monarchs that makes the journey has never been to Mexico, yet they arrive all the same. The next generation may face challenges we have never experienced, but the God who has led us will lead them just the same. That is a hope we can entrust to Him with confidence.

This week, when you face a decision, big or small, please stop and pray for five minutes first, then write down the direction you sense. It might be a choice at work, or whether to say something or not. Five minutes of prayer might save you five months of “recalculating route.”

Brothers and sisters, picture a small monarch taking off in the autumn wind toward a faraway place it has never seen. It does not know the whole route; it only knows which way to fly for the next stretch. But it doesn’t stop, because that direction was placed inside it by the Lord who made it.
Today you may be standing at a crossroads in life, unable to see the road ahead clearly. But the God who helps butterflies, birds and salmon find their way home will surely bring you home too.
Let us quietly reflect: Whose compass is my life following right now?

God who guides, You lead the butterflies and the birds to find their way home; please guide me too. When I cannot see what lies ahead, help me trust You with all my heart and follow You one step at a time. In Jesus’ name, Amen.
1. The monarch’s sun compass, antenna clock and magnetic compass, the migratory bird’s magnetic sense, the salmon’s sense of smell: which amazes you most, and why?
2. Jeremiah says the birds know their seasons, but God’s people don’t know Yahweh’s law. In what areas do you think we today are most likely to “lose our way”?
3. What decision are you facing right now? How are you willing to pray and seek God first this week, letting the Holy Spirit be your guide?
The Waiting of a Seed: After Their Kind, and the Grain of Wheat That Falls
Most certainly I tell you, unless a grain of wheat falls into the earth and dies, it remains by itself alone. But if it dies, it bears much fruit. (John 12:24)

Peace to you, brothers and sisters! Today I’d like you to think for a moment: what is the oldest thing in your home? Some will say Grandma’s old sewing machine, some will say Dad’s radio from his youth, and someone will say, “The oldest thing in my house is that jar of sauce in the fridge. I have no idea when I bought it.”

Well, today I want to introduce a treasure far older than anything in your home. At the site of Masada in Israel, archaeologists dug up a date seed about 2,000 years old. In 2005, someone planted it, and guess what? It actually sprouted, and later grew into a date palm!

Two thousand years ago, when was that? Roughly the time when Jesus walked the earth. That seed slept quietly for two thousand years, waiting until someone planted it in the soil, and then it woke up and said, “Here I am!”
In a dried lakebed in northeastern China, ancient lotus seeds were also unearthed. Radiocarbon dated to about 1,300 years old, they were still able to germinate and grow.
This is the seventh unit of the Life Hall: After Their Kind, Seeds and the Continuity of Life. A tiny seed holds an entire tree and waits for the right time.
1. A Complete Package: God Prepares Everything for Life
Our first point: let’s open up a seed and see what is inside.

Inside a seed is a tiny embryo and a packed supply of nourishment, all wrapped in a protective seed coat. The App puts it charmingly: the embryo is the future plant, the endosperm or cotyledons are its packed lunch, and the seed coat is its armor.

It reminds me of school field trips when I was little. The night before, Mom would start getting ready: lunch packed, water bottle filled, a jacket stuffed into my backpack, worried I’d be cold, hungry or caught in the rain. Every seed is like a child God has carefully packed, with lunch and armor, ready to set out.

The App has another beautiful analogy: a seed is like a sealed letter containing the blueprint of an entire tree, with travel money and armor enclosed. It waits patiently for the moment of delivery, and when the time comes, the letter is opened and the whole tree unfolds from within.

Brothers and sisters, a great tree taller than a house, full of branches and leaves, had its entire blueprint folded up at first inside a seed small enough to rest on your fingertip. That is not magic. That is creation.
What’s more, every seed “follows the rules.” Apple seeds grow apple trees and wheat grows wheat; genetic information is passed down faithfully from generation to generation.
You have never heard of someone planting a watermelon and getting a durian tree, have you? If that ever happened, it would make the news. The Bible records this at its very beginning:
God said, “Let the earth yield grass, herbs yielding seeds, and fruit trees bearing fruit after their kind, with their seeds in it, on the earth;” and it was so. (Genesis 1:11)

“After their kind.” “With their seeds in it.” When God made the plants, He did not make just one generation; He wrapped the power to carry life forward into the seeds within the fruit, to be passed on generation after generation.
2. The Wisdom of Dormancy: Coming Up at the Right Time
Our second point is the thing about seeds I admire most: they know how to wait.
Many seeds do not sprout as soon as they ripen. They wait until temperature, moisture or season is right, so they do not pop up at the wrong time. This is called “dormancy.”
Think about it: if a seed rushed to sprout the moment it fell in autumn, the tender shoot would freeze to death as soon as winter came. So a seed’s waiting is not laziness; it is wisdom.

So how does a seed know when to sleep and when to wake? Scientists have found that dormancy and germination are regulated by plant hormones. In general, a hormone called abscisic acid maintains dormancy, and another called gibberellin promotes germination, and the balance between them responds to signals from the environment.

It is like a car with both a brake and an accelerator. Abscisic acid is the brake, and gibberellin is the accelerator. When the environment isn’t ready, the seed steps on the brake; when the time comes, it steps on the gas. Of course, the details vary by species, and scientists are still studying them.
Roots down first, then the shoot up
When the time comes, the seed absorbs water and swells, and the embryo becomes active. Notice the order: the root goes down first, and then the shoot comes up.

That order is fascinating. The seed doesn’t rush to grow upward so everyone can see its leaves; it first sends roots downward. The unseen part is established first, and only then does the visible part grow.
Brothers and sisters, isn’t our spiritual life the same? Many people want to see results right away and want to be seen right away. But God’s way is often this: first put down roots, then grow tall.
Jesus told a parable about a seed:
and should sleep and rise night and day, and the seed should spring up and grow, he doesn’t know how. (Mark 4:27)

The sower goes to bed and gets up day after day as usual, while the seed sprouts and grows without his even knowing it. Much of life’s growth happens when we cannot see it. You may have prayed for someone for a long time, and it seems nothing has happened, but perhaps the seed has already quietly sprouted underground.
After the Flood, God made a promise to humanity:
While the earth remains, seed time and harvest, and cold and heat, and summer and winter, and day and night will not cease. (Genesis 8:22)

Every sowing and every harvest speaks of God’s faithfulness. The two-thousand-year-old date seed and the thirteen-hundred-year-old lotus seeds are telling us that the life God placed in seeds is more resilient and more faithful than we imagine. The way seeds precisely prepare for, wait for and pass on life makes it reasonable for us to infer that there is a faithful, farsighted Creator behind them. This is a philosophical inference, but a very warm one.
3. The Grain of Wheat That Falls: Only by Dying Does It Bear Much Fruit
Jesus used a seed to explain Himself
Our third point is today’s most important message. Jesus used a seed to explain His own death and resurrection:
Most certainly I tell you, unless a grain of wheat falls into the earth and dies, it remains by itself alone. But if it dies, it bears much fruit. (John 12:24)
If a grain of wheat stays in the barn, however well it is preserved, it will only ever be one grain. It must fall into the ground and its outer shell must break open before new life can grow.

Jesus is that grain of wheat. He gave Himself up and was buried; His body seemed broken, and everyone thought it was all over. But He rose again and bore the fruit of countless saved lives. Every Christian here today is one of the grains that single grain of wheat produced.
Not made alive unless it dies
Paul used the same principle to speak of the resurrection:
You foolish one, that which you yourself sow is not made alive unless it dies. (1 Corinthians 15:36)

This is also the path for those who follow Jesus. Our old self, our pride, our selfishness, our insistence on our own rights also need to fall into the ground and die. That sounds painful, but remember: the death of a seed is not the end; it is the beginning. Only by dying can it grow into a life far greater than itself.
Sometimes we cling tightly to things and refuse to let go: my reputation, my plans, my rights. We are like that grain of wheat kept in the barn, well preserved, yet forever only one grain.
God invites us to place these things in His hands and let them fall into the ground. When we are willing to let go, God can bring forth much fruit in us.
The first application is to deny yourself. Unless a grain of wheat dies, it remains alone. When we lay down our own rights, life multiplies.

This is the same as what 321 calls “selflessness,” the self-emptied life: no longer centered on ourselves, but letting Christ live in us. At home, it might mean being the first to apologize; at church, it might mean being willing to give up your seat. Every act of self-denial is a grain of wheat falling into the ground.
The second application is multiplication. The purpose of a seed is to produce more seeds. We too must pass the gospel and our lives on to the next person.

An apple tree does not bear fruit to look good for itself, but to pass life on. A Christian’s life is not only about being saved ourselves; it is about becoming a blessing to the next person. Today you are the fruit of a seed someone else sowed; tomorrow you must become a sower too.
The eight steps of changing our mindset: repetition
The third application is “repetition,” one of the eight steps of changing our mindset in 321. A seed needs waiting and watering, and a changed life also needs repeated practice.

You wouldn’t plant a seed and then dig it up the next day to check whether it has grown, would you? Then it would never grow. Changing our lives is the same: it needs daily watering and daily sunshine, reading Scripture, praying and practicing again and again. When the time comes, it will sprout and bear fruit.

This week, please plant a bean in a cup and watch how it changes each day. At the same time, pray for a friend you want to share the gospel with. Each time you look at the bean, pray for your friend once. Perhaps after a week, when the bean has sprouted, the seed in your friend’s heart will have begun to sprout too.
Brothers and sisters, please hold a seed in your palm; it can be a grain of rice, a bean or a fruit pit. Think about the whole plant hidden inside it.
It is so small, yet it holds so much life; it is so quiet, yet it knows how to wait for the right time; it is willing to fall into the ground, and so it can bear much fruit.
Let us quietly reflect: What in my life needs to “fall into the earth and die” so that God can bring forth more fruit?

Faithful Lord, You are the grain of wheat that fell into the earth and laid down Your life for me. Make me willing to deny myself as well, to let my old self die, so that Your life in me may bear much fruit. In Jesus’ name, Amen.
