Three Legs Go Farther: Symbiosis, Ecology and Completing One Another
so we, who are many, are one body in Christ, and individually members of one another. (Romans 12:5)

Peace to you, brothers and sisters! Have any of you ever run a three-legged race? It is one of the liveliest events at a school sports day. Two people stand side by side, tie their inside legs together, and then run forward shouting, “One, two, one, two!”

When I was a kid, I was paired with a classmate, and we both had strong personalities. He wanted to lead with his left foot, and I wanted to lead with my right. We hadn’t gone two steps before we both fell flat on the track, and the whole crowd burst out laughing. Then our teacher told us, “Don’t each go your own way. Look at each other and call out the rhythm together.” We practiced a few times, got in step, and to our surprise we ran faster and farther than either of us could alone.

The App uses this very analogy: symbiosis is like a three-legged race. Two people have their legs tied together. If each goes their own way, they fall; when they move in step, they can go farther than either could alone.

Today is the final unit of the Life Hall, and our topic is “Completing One Another: Symbiosis and Ecology.” We are going to see how, in the world God made, figs and wasps, corals and algae, trees and fungi need each other and complete one another.
Our key verse is Romans 12:5: “so we, who are many, are one body in Christ, and individually members of one another.”
1. Figs and Fig Wasps: You Need Me, and I Need You
Our first point looks at a very special pair of partners. Did you know that figs actually have flowers? It’s just that their flowers are hidden inside the fruit, so bees and butterflies can’t get in.
So who pollinates them? The only creature that can is a fig wasp smaller than a grain of rice.

The female wasp squeezes in through a tiny opening at the tip of the fig, pollinates the flowers inside, and lays her eggs there. Her offspring grow up inside the fruit, then fly off carrying pollen to find the next fig. And so the fig needs the wasp, and the wasp needs the fig.

It is practically a heartwarming family story: the fig provides a home for the wasp’s children, and the wasp helps the fig carry on its family line. Each gives to the other, and each receives from the other.
Of the more than 700 species of figs worldwide, most have their own dedicated pollinating wasp, and neither can reproduce without the other.

Still, scientists have found that although these one-to-one pairings are common, there are many exceptions: sometimes one fig species has several wasp species, and sometimes one wasp species serves several fig species. I appreciate that honesty. Nature is richer than we imagine, and scientists are willing to revise simple accounts.
Scripture: I have no need for you?
Paul says something very vivid in 1 Corinthians:
The eye can’t tell the hand, “I have no need for you,” or again the head to the feet, “I have no need for you.” (1 Corinthians 12:21)

Imagine if one day the fig said, “I have no need for you little bugs.” It would never produce another generation. And if the wasp said, “I don’t need the fig; I’m doing just fine on my own,” its children would have nowhere to grow up.

It is the same in the church. Sometimes we say in our hearts, “That person and I don’t get along. I have no need for them.” But God put us in the same body precisely so that we would understand: needing one another is not weakness; it is design.
2. Corals and Symbiotic Algae: Good Roommates

Our second point takes us down to the seafloor to look at coral. Tiny algae live inside the coral’s body. The algae photosynthesize and supply nutrients to the coral, and the coral provides a home and raw materials for the algae.

It is like a shared house. The landlord coral says, “You can live here rent-free, but would you cook for me every day?” The algae say, “Sure! Cooking with sunlight is my specialty.” And so these two good roommates build the beautiful coral reefs of the sea together.

But even these good roommates sometimes split up. When seawater gets too hot, the coral, under heat stress, expels its symbiotic algae and turns white. This is called “coral bleaching.” If it lasts too long, the coral may die.

Brothers and sisters, this is a deep reminder for me. When pressure gets too great, the easiest thing for us to do is push away the very partners we need most. Work gets stressful, so we stop going to small group; we feel down, so we stop answering our friends’ calls. We think we are protecting ourselves, but in fact we are letting our lives “bleach.”
Under pressure, what we need is to draw closer to one another, not push one another away.
Scripture: two are better than one
Two are better than one, because they have a good reward for their labor. (Ecclesiastes 4:9)
Corals and algae labor together and build gardens under the sea. When we labor together with our brothers and sisters, we too can build a beautiful testimony in this world.
3. Cooperation Underground: Mycorrhizae and the Forest
A trade between roots and fungi

Our third point brings us back to land to look underground. The roots of most land plants partner with fungi, and this is called “mycorrhiza.” The fungi help the plants absorb water and minerals such as phosphorus, and the plants repay the fungi with sugars.

Look: plants can make sugar through photosynthesis but aren’t very good at hunting around for water and minerals; fungi are great at burrowing through the soil for resources but can’t make their own sugar. When they work together, each contributes its strengths and covers the other’s weaknesses. It is like a company where some people are good at sales and others at accounting; only when they work together does the company run.
A wood wide web? Let’s be honest

A 1997 study showed that carbon can be transferred between different trees through underground mycorrhizal networks. That sparked many people’s imaginations about a “wood wide web,” as though there were an internet beneath the forest floor.

However, a 2023 review pointed out that many claims about “mother trees feeding young trees through the network” have been overinterpreted, and the evidence remains limited. How much common mycorrhizal networks in forests actually transfer between trees, and what ecological significance they have, is still disputed.

Brothers and sisters, I especially want to mention this. Sometimes a very moving claim circulates online, and we really want to use it as a sermon illustration. But as Christians who love the truth, we must distinguish between what has evidence and what has been exaggerated. Some effects have evidence, but they are often overinterpreted; that is the honest way to put it. We don’t need to exaggerate. God’s works are wonderful enough as they are.
Scripture: ask the animals, ask the birds

“But ask the animals, now, and they shall teach you; the birds of the sky, and they shall tell you. Or speak to the earth, and it shall teach you. The fish of the sea shall declare to you. Who doesn’t know that in all these, Yahweh’s hand has done this, (Job 12:7–9)

The fig and the wasp are speaking, the coral and the algae are speaking, and the roots and the fungi are speaking too. Together they declare that this world is not a collection of isolated parts but a web of connections. The intricate relationships in which living things complete one another make it reasonable for us to infer that there is a wise Creator who makes all things work together. This is a philosophical inference, but all of creation seems to bear witness to it.
Looking back over the whole Life Hall

Having walked through the eight units of the Life Hall, what have we seen? From the written code of DNA, the city of the cell and molecular motors, to protein folding, the source of life, navigating birds, the grain of wheat that falls to the ground, and creatures that complete one another, God’s wisdom and goodness are everywhere. Paul put it well:

For the invisible things of him since the creation of the world are clearly seen, being perceived through the things that are made, even his everlasting power and divinity, that they may be without excuse. (Romans 1:20)
That is what “Creation Speaks” is all about. We are not searching nature for the answer to a proof problem; we are recognizing, in all things, the Lord who gives life and eternal life.
920: living the self-emptied life in relationships

The first application is 920, the fruit of the Spirit in Galatians 5:22–23. Live the self-emptied life in your relationships and bear the fruit of the Spirit, just as symbiotic partners complete one another.

The fig does not flower for itself, and the wasp does not fly only for itself. Selfless people in relationships don’t ask, “What can I get?” but “What can I help bring to completion?” When we live this way, the fruit of the Spirit grows naturally in our relationships.
The second application is “relationships matter more than things.” Our greatest resource is not what we own but who we walk with.

A coral’s most precious possession is not its skeleton but the algae that live with it; a tree’s most precious possession may not be its wood but the fungi working with it in the soil. The most precious thing in our lives is not our savings or our titles but the people God has placed beside us to walk with us.
The third application is 235 comrades in arms, a small band who stand together. Find companions to fight alongside you, for a threefold cord is not quickly broken.

A believer on their own can easily “bleach” under pressure; with comrades in arms walking alongside, we can support and remind one another. Don’t be a lonely tree; be part of a forest where everyone is connected.

This week, please write a card to someone who has “completed” you in your life, thank them, and tell them you are praying for them. It might be your spouse, a spiritual companion of many years, or a friend who has quietly supported you. That card is like the rhythm you call out together in a three-legged race: “Let’s go together.”

Brothers and sisters, congratulations on completing the Life Hall! From the language of DNA, the city of the cell and molecular machines, to navigating birds, the grain of wheat that falls to the ground and the creatures that complete one another, you have seen God’s wisdom, goodness and faithfulness displayed throughout life, and you have come to know the Lord who gives life and eternal life.
Now think about it: who in your life is like your “symbiotic partner”? What have you received from them, and what have you given them?
Let us quietly reflect: Do I often think, “I have no need for you”? Am I willing to admit that I need other people?

Lord who gives life, thank You for placing me in Your body so that I need not be alone. Make me humble enough to accept help and glad to help others grow, building one another up in love with my brothers and sisters. In Jesus’ name, Amen.
